rewritten_text:
In my younger days, discontent never entered my mind. If boredom ever overcame me, the beauty of the natural world or the study of humanity's finest and most sublime creations could always engage my heart and restore my spirits. But I am a tree shattered by lightning; the bolt has struck my soul. I felt then that I would live on to display what I shall soon no longer be: a miserable example of ruined humanity, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent a considerable time at Oxford, wandering through the surrounding countryside and trying to identify every place connected with the most inspiring period of English history. Each new object of interest often drew out our little journeys of discovery. We visited the tomb of the distinguished Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment, my soul rose above its degrading, wretched fears to contemplate the divine ideals of freedom and self-sacrifice commemorated by these places. For an instant, I dared to throw off my chains and look around with a free and elevated spirit. But the iron had bitten into my flesh, and I sank back into my miserable self, trembling and hopeless.

We were sorry to leave Oxford and continued to Matlock, our next stopping place. The countryside near this village more closely resembled Switzerland's scenery, though everything was on a smaller scale. The green hills lacked the crown of distant white Alps that always rises beyond the pine-covered mountains of my native country. We explored the marvellous cave and the small natural-history collections, where the curiosities were arranged as they are in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry spoke that latter name, I trembled, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which had thus become linked in my mind with that terrible scene.

Traveling north from Derby, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. Here I could almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains. The little patches of snow still clinging to the mountains' northern slopes, the lakes, and the rush of streams over rocks were all familiar, beloved sights. We also made acquaintances who almost managed to lure me into happiness. Clerval's delight was correspondingly greater than my own. His mind broadened in the company of talented men, and he discovered within himself abilities and resources greater than anything he could have imagined possessing when his companions had been less gifted than he was.

‘Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean Sir Simon—are you hungry? I've got a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?’

‘No, thank you. I never eat now. But it's very kind of you all the same, and you're much nicer than the rest of your horrible, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.’

‘Stop!’ cried Virginia, stamping her foot. ‘You're the one who's rude and horrible and vulgar. And if we're talking about dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to freshen up that ridiculous bloodstain in the library. First you took all my reds, even the vermilion, so I couldn't paint any more sunsets. Then you took the emerald green and chrome yellow. In the end, I had only indigo and Chinese white left, so I could paint nothing but moonlight scenes, which are always depressing to look at and very difficult to paint. I never told anyone, even though I was terribly annoyed. And the whole thing was utterly ridiculous. Who ever heard of emerald-green blood?’

‘Well, really,’ said the Ghost, rather meekly, ‘what else could I do? Real blood is very hard to get these days. Besides, your brother started everything with his Paragon Detergent, so I saw no reason not to use your paints. As for colour, that's always a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, for instance—the bluest in England. But I know you Americans don't value that sort of thing.’

‘You know nothing about it. The best thing you could do is move abroad and broaden your mind. My father would be delighted to pay your fare. Although there's a heavy tax on spirits of every kind, you wouldn't have any trouble at Customs, since the officers are all Democrats. Once you reached New York, you'd certainly be a great success. I know plenty of people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars for a grandfather, and much more for a family ghost.’

‘I don't think I'd like America.’

‘Because we haven't any ruins or curiosities, I suppose,’ Virginia said sarcastically.

‘No ruins! No curiosities!’ the Ghost replied. ‘You have your navy and your manners.’

‘Good evening. I'll ask Papa to give the twins an extra week's holiday.’

‘Please don't go, Miss Virginia,’ he cried. ‘I'm so lonely and unhappy, and I really don't know what to do. I want to sleep, but I can't.’

‘That's absurd! All you need to do is get into bed and blow out the candle.’

The insect's weight was truly extraordinary, and, all things considered, I could scarcely fault Jupiter for his belief concerning it; but why Legrand should share that belief I could not, for the life of me, understand.

‘I summoned you,’ he said pompously, once I had finished examining the beetle, ‘I summoned you so that I might obtain your advice and assistance in advancing the designs of Fate and of the bug—’

‘My dear Legrand,’ I exclaimed, cutting him short, ‘you are undoubtedly ill and ought to take a few precautions. You must go to bed, and I shall stay here for several days until this passes. You are feverish and—’

‘Take my pulse,’ he said.

I did so, and, in truth, detected not the least sign of fever.

‘Still, you can be ill without having a fever. Let me prescribe for you this once. First, go to bed. Then—’

‘You are wrong,’ he interrupted. ‘I am as well as one could expect under the excitement I am enduring. If you truly wish to help me, you will ease that excitement.’

‘And how can I do that?’

‘Quite simply. Jupiter and I intend to make an expedition into the hills on the mainland, and we shall require the assistance of someone in whom we have confidence. You are the only person we can trust. Success or failure will alike quiet the excitement you observe in me.’

‘I am eager to oblige you however I can,’ I answered; ‘but are you saying that this infernal beetle has anything to do with your journey into the hills?’

‘It has.’

‘Then, Legrand, I cannot participate in so absurd an undertaking.’

‘I am sorry—exceedingly sorry—for we must attempt it alone.’

‘Attempt it alone! Surely the man is mad! But wait—how long do you expect to be away?’

‘Likely the entire night. We shall leave at once and return, in any case, by sunrise.’

‘And will you pledge your honor that, once this whim is over and the bug affair—good God!—settled to your satisfaction, you will come home and obey my advice without question, as though I were your physician?’

‘Yes, I promise. Now let us go; there is no time to spare.’

With a troubled heart I went with my friend. We set out at about four o'clock: Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and I. Jupiter brought the scythe and spades, insisting on carrying every one of them. This seemed to me less a sign of unusual diligence or willingness to oblige than of his fear of leaving either sort of implement within his master's reach.
